text:
The Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol was launched by Google in April 2025 to enable seamless communication and collaboration between AI agents, addressing interoperability issues within multi-agent systems. On June 23, 2025, Google announced at the North American Open Source Summit that it would donate the A2A project to the Linux Foundation to ensure neutral governance. The donation is supported by over 100 technology companies including Amazon, Cisco, Microsoft, Salesforce, Atlassian, Box, LangChain, ServiceNow, and others. Industry support for the protocol grew significantly after its launch; as of April 9, 2026, more than 150 organizations were supporting the standard with active production deployments across industries such as supply chain management, financial services, insurance, and IT operations. By early 2026, the core GitHub repository had surpassed 22,000 stars and the SDK ecosystem expanded to include five production-ready languages: Python, JavaScript, Java, Go, and .NET.

A primary distinction between A2A and other protocols like Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP) is their specific focus areas within AI interoperability. MCP was introduced in late 2024 and focuses on connecting AI models to external tools and data sources, effectively solving the challenge of integrating diverse data systems into agent workflows. In contrast, A2A enables agents themselves to communicate directly with one another regardless of whether they were built by different vendors or use different underlying frameworks. This allows for peer-to-peer task delegation where an agent can discover capabilities via Agent Cards—JSON metadata documents published at well-known URIs—and coordinate actions across enterprise systems without exposing internal memory or proprietary logic. The protocol supports multiple communication methods including request-response polling, Server-Sent Events (SSE) for streaming updates during short-running tasks, and push notifications for long-running operations.

Despite its rapid adoption and industry backing, researchers have identified several security vulnerabilities in the original A2A specification that require mitigation strategies such as explicit user consent orchestration and ephemeral token management. Critical weaknesses include insufficient control over token lifetime, a lack of strong customer authentication mechanisms, overly granular access scopes, and potential excessive exposure of sensitive data to agents executing tasks on behalf of users. These gaps increase risks related to unauthorized disclosure, privilege escalation, and misuse of private information within generative multi-agent environments. To address these concerns, an enhanced version of the protocol was proposed featuring direct data flow controllers between users and services, reducing reliance on agent-mediated data transmission for high-value transactions like payment processing or identity verification.

The Linux Foundation's governance structure aims to prevent vendor lock-in by ensuring A2A remains neutral while fostering community-driven innovation through contributions from major cloud providers including Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure AI Foundry, Copilot Studio, and AWS Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. While some industry observers note potential challenges such as slower decision-making due to complex multi-party governance processes and conflicts of interest arising when different companies prioritize competing development directions, current evidence suggests that benefits regarding standardization, modularity, and accelerated innovation outweigh these risks. The protocol has successfully moved beyond early adoption phases into widespread enterprise use cases where specialized agents collaborate on complex workflows spanning multiple organizational boundaries.
